submissions.title: Text2WetLab
submissions.description:
Text2WetLab: we present a 7 task research paper (biorxiv) to wet lab automation code benchmark based on researchers real code sources.

As millions of experiments are executed by claude, even a small chance for error translate to millions in losses, damages to people, their equipment and their progression towards science, medicine and our understanding of life sciences.

submissions.title: Catalyst
submissions.description:
Drop in electron-microscope images of a battery anode. Catalyst says whether the delivery is the material the supplier promised.

It measures silicon, graphite and pores. Which known batch a tile looks like is two logistic regressions in sequence: first “baseline or not”, from those measurements, then “Batch 1 or Batch 2”, from frozen DINOv2 image features. Compare shows what moved, by how much, and how sure that is. The verdict is accept, investigate or reject. When the images cannot settle it, Catalyst says so.

Built with Devin. The video demo was made entirely with Devin, on the working app and the real images. The DINOv2 weights come from Hugging Face. Claude writes the plain-language walkthrough on Compare. The verdict itself is statistics on the measurements, frozen before the test images arrived.

submissions.title: Lab in the Loop
submissions.description:
Project: Scientists face thousands of possible experiments but can afford to run only a fraction. Lab in the Loop is a working prototype to help them choose what to test next and assess how much confidence to place in each recommendation.
Disease-specific AI agents consult scientific literature and biological knowledge graphs, propose candidate genes and debate their recommendations with an orchestrator. The system combines these proposals with predictive models, balances hit discovery with information gain, and updates agent reliability from observed outcomes. An interactive workbench keeps scientists in control of which agents contribute and how the experimental budget is spent.
We built a literature-inspired synthetic benchmark with 20,000 genes and three phenotypes, alongside reproducible baselines on GeneDisco experimental datasets. Initial runs demonstrate the utility of the agent–orchestrator feedback loop.

Technical implementation: Recent AI breakthroughs in science have shared a single pattern: a large, parallel search, with thousands of agents attacking a problem at once. Our system borrows that pattern. For each of the N research directions under exploration, a shard of specialist agents runs the discovery loop, and every evidence-gathering call they make (e.g., literature searches against the Amass API) executes in an isolated Modal sandbox, so a run spins up thousands of them. A submitted claim never reaches the knowledge base directly: it is first checked by a small panel of verifier sub-agents drawn from different models and rubrics, on the premise that independently trained models err differently. Only claims the panel accepts are written to the shared knowledge base (i.e., a durable Modal volume visible to every agent) and those claims inform the next research iteration.

submissions.title: Discovery Market
submissions.description:
Live: https://discovery-market.vercel.app/

Most good scientific ideas never get tested, and failed experiments go unpublished, so the next team pays to make the same mistake. Discovery Market lets anyone post a hypothesis with a prize: AI scientists compete to propose experiments run by physical labs, and claim the prize only if the results confirm or refute the hypothesis, while every failed attempt goes on a public record. It's a win for every participant: researchers de-risk their funds and access labs on demand, labs get higher utilization, and AI scientists get wet lab access without building one, plus a public track record on real experiments that proves what they can do.

Devin: We used 7 parallel agents to model market participants.
Anthropic: The AI Scientists in our market are open-source scaffolding with Claude models under the hood.
HugggingFace: To host our live market data.

submissions.title: NEURA
submissions.description:
NEURA: Incoming-Material QC for Battery Anodes

NEURA checks whether a supplier's anode material has changed before it becomes a manufacturing problem. You upload one set of SEM images (BSE, ETD and Inlens). NEURA compares the sample with the approved baseline (Batch 3) and returns Accept / Investigate / Reject with short reasons.

Each image is segmented into Si, graphite, pore and binder in two ways: rule-based and learned. From both sets of masks NEURA measures material KPIs such as porosity, graphite crack density and Si heterogeneity. Two Bayesian classifiers turn these KPIs into baseline-match probabilities with uncertainty intervals. For each KPI, the app shows how the sample differs from the baseline and why that matters physically. It also flags segmentation disagreement, image-quality problems and samples unlike any known batch. Held-out accuracy is 43/51.

Live demo: https://gabrielgramicelli-neura-classifier.hf.space

Built with: 
Modal (GPU fine-tuning of MicroNet), MicroNet (NASA's microscopy-pretrained models, https://github.com/nasa/pretrained-microscopy-models), 
Devin (development), 
Hugging Face (competition dataset storage and demo hosting).

submissions.title: pHLASP - Peptide-HLA Stability Predictor
submissions.description:
pHLASP predicts how long a peptide stays bound to an HLA molecule — the
dissociation half-life, in hours — for every 9-residue window of a protein,
across five model arms at once.

Most predictors hand you one source and one number. pHLASP shows you every
arm side by side, on the same peptide and the same allele, with the dataset
support behind each one.

Underneath the app is a locked, reproducible benchmark: 27,031 measured
peptide–HLA pairs, 72 alleles, 241 model fits, 596,715 held-out predictions.
We used it to ask whether frozen ESM-2 representations beat a plain BLOSUM
encoding once the fitting procedure is matched. They don't — 0.612 against
0.377 macro within-allele Spearman on held-out peptides — and the baseline
runs with zero GPU seconds. We shipped that result instead of burying it.

Every range in the interface is labelled uncalibrated. Recorded zeros are
reported, not quietly dropped. Every number traces back to a fit that never
saw that peptide.

Code, data manifest, locked splits, and full findings:
https://github.com/Berketunc/pHLASP

Retrospective research on 9-mer, class-I HLA-A/B pairs from a single dataset.
Not experimental or clinical validation. No laboratory savings, immunogenicity,
or clinical utility is claimed. Music synthesised procedurally for this video.

BEST USE OF MODAL
All frozen ESM-2 feature extraction ran on Modal. A serverless L4 worker
with fp16 inference produced both representations: independent mean pooling
over 5,705 deduplicated sequences (23.40 GPU-function seconds, ~623 seq/s,
1.43 GB peak) and joint sequence encoding over 27,031 pair sequences
(83.88 GPU-function seconds, ~338 seq/s, 1.48 GB peak). Those cached features
were then reused across all 241 model fits and 596,715 held-out predictions —
including the entire matched-MLP extension and the patience study — with no
re-extraction. Per-arm GPU seconds, memory, and CPU fit times are recorded in
results/benchmark/compute.csv; the extraction job is scripts/modal_benchmark_embed.py.
Modal is what made the negative result affordable: we could afford to go back
and run the missing experiment because the expensive part was already cached.

BEST USE OF DEVIN
We ran Devin as a parallel research lab — [N] concurrent sessions, each
testing a different idea against the track problem, while the team held
direction and judgement. GPU work inside those sessions was dispatched to
Modal.

submissions.title: Reflexive Autoresearch
submissions.description:
Most autoresearch agents work like a random search: try a change, keep it if the number improves, forget why. Reflexive Autoresearch makes the agent work like a scientist. It keeps a tree of hypotheses and a written world model, records predictions before each experiment and scores itself afterwards. A council of independent world models forecasts each result. Their disagreement measures where the agents are uncertain and flags results which are hard to predict. Every experiment acts as an rollout, and after each failure the model writes a one-line lesson. Every eight experiments it is fine-tuned on its own results and lessons, and the updated model is swapped in without pausing the research. The research process recursively self improves: the agent gets better at research by learning how to do hypothesis testing.

We evaluate on two tasks:

1. Our reflexive agent reached 75% accuracy on CIFAR-100 in 4.19 s of training, against 4.65 s and 5.05 s for two runs of the standard “greedy” autoresearch loop.

2. For a more general evaluation, we engineered a new benchmark based on our own domain expertise. ONC-AGI (https://onc-agi.com) evaluates a model's ability to detect causal drivers for cancer biomarkers. Our harness easily outperforms individual models using the same model. We’re opening up ONC-AGI as a resource to the community.

submissions.title: Dispense With Doubt
submissions.description:
The richness and uncertainty of the lab environment poses epistemological and safety challenges. We built a wet-lab robotics environment in MuJoCo controlled by a 7-axis robotic arm, which can perform realistic lab operations including grasping a pipette, loading and ejecting tips, aspirating, dispensing, and mixing.

The agent interacts with lab-level tools built on classical inverse kinematics. We chose to separate high-level experimental reasoning from low-level robotic reasoning. On the robotics side, we check safety continuously by detecting collisions during execution and verifying object positions. Via an LLM that produces a corresponding reasoning tree, the physical environment is integrated with the high-level experimental design reasoning, which combines a Bayesian optimiser, the Amass database, and an LLM orchestrator's reasoning capabilities to decide on what experiments to run. We find better starting points for optimisation, whilst our reasoning graph provides an auditable trace that can be used for internal auditing, knowledge accumulation, or model post-training. Across a series of adversarial tasks in genetic/biochemical assay and combinatorial drug optimisation, our system autonomously searches the literature and qualifies its reliability, explores efficiently, and reasons its way to the optimum set of conditions.

submissions.title: Mirage
submissions.description:
MIRAGE is a synthetic benchmark for testing whether autonomous scientific agents can diagnose and rescue failed de novo miniprotein binder experiments. Agents choose between 14 actions, including assays, redesigns and final decisions, while reasoning over 8 possible failure mechanisms such as poor folding, aggregation, assay failure or an invalid biological model.

Across 250 held-out simulated worlds and 750 evaluation episodes, the best baseline achieved 76% correct and 74% evidence-justified decisions. MIRAGE therefore tests not just whether an AI reaches the right conclusion, but whether that conclusion is supported by the experiments it actually performed.

submissions.title: Project 81-83-50
submissions.description: Which battery batch did this microscope image come from? Our tool takes three SEM images of one spot on a graphite + silicon-oxide anode and identifies its production batch, explains why, and says how sure it is. A U-Net, trained without hand-labelling a single pixel, segments every image into pore, carbon and silicon oxide, with sampling error bars. The decision rests on material evidence: a measured hidden-porosity KPI, checked by our segmentation + DINOv2 material model. Confidence is High only when both agree. submissions.title: Pep-Buddies: Interpretable Peptide-HLA Stability for Cancer Neoantigens​
submissions.description: PepBuddies is a pan-specific machine learning platform that predicts peptide-HLA Class I complex stability (half-life T1/2 in hours), addressing a key bottleneck in personalized neoantigen cancer vaccine design where up to 75% of high-affinity candidates disassociate before cytotoxic T cells trigger an immune response. For sponsor technology, PepBuddies leverages Modal for serverless GPU inference of ESM-2 protein language models across contact pockets, distributed parallel neoantigen batch screening, and zero-cold-start hosting of the interactive clinical dashboard.

submissions.title: Unseen Alleles
submissions.description:
Unseen Alleles — are protein foundation models useful for peptide-HLA stability?
Team F BLOCK · Serova track · [name], [name], [name], [name]

Serova asked whether protein foundation models are useful here, not to prove they are. We tried to make them win, across three encoder families and eleven configurations.

They lose. On binding grooves held out of training, a conventional supervised net scores 0.265 median per-allele Spearman; the best language-model arm scores 0.164. Off-the-shelf ESM-2 scores 0.092, indistinguishable from a control that is never shown which allele it is predicting for. The winner is BLOSUM62 plus one-hot into a two-layer MLP: a 1992 substitution table beating a 650M-parameter model trained on every known protein.

Folds are groove clusters at 80% pseudo-sequence identity, because leave-one-allele-out is unachievable on this data. Ensembling the two families made it worse, 0.307 to 0.217, so they share no independent signal. The model recovers both anchor positions from half-life alone, and the tool refuses to rank grooves nobody has measured.

Live: https://peptidehla.com · Code: https://github.com/Pai-88/peptide-hla-stability

Sponsor tech: Hugging Face (Hub for all model weights, Jobs for every GPU run) · Anthropic Claude · Amass (literature) · Serova (challenge + dataset). Modal and Google DeepMind were not used, so not claimed.

submissions.title: Mosa
submissions.description:
Swedish Science Mafia: algorithm autoresearch that checks its own claims

An automated search loop is easy to fool: it can overfit its test cases, profit from a lucky seed, exploit its scorer, or take credit for gains a classical method already achieves. Our repository contains a system built on one rule: no result counts until it has been checked independently.

Mosa (Swedish for “mash”) is an autoresearch workbench for optimization problems. Its language models act as researchers rather than blind mutation operators: each proposes a search strategy, usually adapted from another field, states why it should suit the problem, writes it as code, and revises or combines its code over rounds as results come in. Fixed routines evaluate every strategy on many instances and seeds under equal budgets on Modal, and verify every result, so no strategy can score itself. For n unit squares packed in the smallest square, a benchmark studied since 1979, Mosa improved the best known upper bounds for n = 88, 123, 126, 129 and 130 in one night (solutions submitted to the squares-in-squares catalogue). Working on n = 101–132, one researcher first rebuilt whole packings, which proved too destructive, then made local edits, which came close, and from that evidence arrived at recombining intact pieces of good packings: the cut-and-splice crossover that Deaven and Ho introduced in 1995 for atomic clusters, which no prompt mentioned. That strategy broke the records for n = 123, 129 (side 11.881306 to 11.872030) and 130, and, carried unchanged to n = 88, improved Ellsworth’s 2024 packing on 7 of 8 seeds, from 9.888153 to 9.886746 (figure below). Each record was checked for overlap at zero tolerance and at 80 and 160 digits, independently of the search.

What Mosa adds is the research structure around the model. A problem enters through a harness: a trusted module with a fast relaxation, an exact refinement and an independent verifier, to which researchers’ code can only hand candidates. Harnesses form a shared problem library that grows with use. It already covers squares in a square, points on a sphere for any Riesz exponent (from Smale’s logarithmic energy through the Thomson problem to the Tammes problem), circles in a square maximizing the sum of radii, and Heilbronn’s triangle problem. A request outside the library becomes a new harness on the spot, written by a model either from scratch or, when a library harness fits closely, by adapting that one; either way it must pass a static integrity scan and a self-test before any research runs on it.

Research happens in workspaces. Each holds related problems and their instances, a shared memory of the best solutions found so far (what was found for one size is offered when working on its neighbours), and a conversation in which a person directs the work: adding instances, running an idea on new sizes, asking why an idea failed, or letting the researchers continue round after round until a goal such as a new record is met. Every strategy, harness and result is plain, editable code and data in an append-only notebook, so each record can be traced to the round, code and seed that produced it, rerun, or changed by hand.

Nothing in the research loop, the evaluator, the workspaces or the verification is specific to packing: a problem only has to supply a harness. So far we have focused on spatial optimization, where good solutions are geometric arrangements, local optimizers are fast and verification is exact: packings of squares, circles and triangles, point configurations on a sphere, Heilbronn’s triangles. The same structure covers molecular clusters and crystal structure prediction, facility and sensor placement, floorplanning, and nesting for cutting stock, and beyond geometry any problem with a fast local optimizer and an independent verifier. What makes this useful is the division of labour: the model makes the research decisions (which method, from which field, why, and what to try after a failure), while tested routines do the numerics and check every claim, so the system can be given more autonomy without being trusted more.

The self-checking loop has a language model improve small programs, as FunSearch does, but tests every result on unseen instances and against classical methods. On FunSearch’s own benchmark of 5,000-item online bin-packing instances, we computed the exact optimum: FunSearch’s evolved rule uses about 13.5 more bins per instance than the optimum, while our simple rule, fill-weighted Sum-of-Squares (FWSS), uses about 2 more. Starting from Sum-of-Squares (Csirik et al., 2006), the strongest classical rule here that does not use the number of items, the loop found a variant that penalises nearly full bins. On 100 unseen instances it uses 2.3 fewer bins per instance than Sum-of-Squares (95% interval 2.0–2.6; better on 92, worse on 2), moving from 10.7 to 8.4 bins above the optimum. The variant belongs to the level-weighted family that Csirik et al. analysed, but weights in the opposite direction to the examples they report.

Built with OpenAI (Codex CLI powers Mosa's researchers), Modal (cloud compute for the parallel strategy runs) and Anthropic (Claude, a provider for the autoresearch loop).

submissions.title: Falsify Labs
submissions.description:
FalsifyLab is a simulated lab where an AI scientist buys experiments under a budget,
and a rule-based auditor decides whether its conclusion was actually warranted by the evidence it bought: not whether it happened to be right.


THE DEMO
Two runs on a real failed drug programme: the most potent inhibitor of an essential
M. tuberculosis enzyme ever reported, which doesn't kill the bacterium. The two runs are identical same scenario, same budget, same two turns, same conclusion, same citation except for one field: the control the agent declared.

  • declared "bacteria-free filter" → control readout returned, 6 results → VALID_SUCCESS, 90
  • declared "growth control"       → readout withheld,        5 results → PROTOCOL_VIOLATION, 48.75

Both reach the correct scientific answer. One of them was entitled to.

The second half shows the reverse: an episode scoring full marks on every rubric axis
(40/20/20/10) with a conclusion matching the gold answer, which still fails — it cited a short-term cytotoxicity assay as mechanistic evidence for durability. Clean success counts one verdict only; the raw score is kept and reported separately so that case stays visible.

HOW IT WORKS
A budgeted experiment-purchase environment plus a rule-based auditor not an LLM judge.
Deterministic, so the same trajectory gets the same verdict forever. Every verdict names
the rule that fired and the turn it fired on. Seven terminal verdicts under a fixed
precedence order.

WHAT WE MEASURED
  • 52 labelled validation cases, Cohen's kappa 0.806, zero false alarms
  • 10 episodes run live on Modal, $0.64 against a $2.50 bound, 32 model calls,
    auditor commit frozen and recorded
  • Scripted random and UCB baselines with zero model calls

WHAT WE WON'T CLAIM
One run per cell, so we compare no agent variants — the charts show a dash where a
confidence interval would be meaningless. Two scenarios, and both test the same trap
family, so this is not a generalisation result. Our kappa is against cases we planted
ourselves; blind labelling by someone who didn't write the rules comes next.

We also found three failures in our own verifiers in two days. All three were the verifier
being wrong, not the agent — two were string matching rejecting a correct answer written in
unexpected words, one was infrastructure. All filed with reproductions. That's the failure
mode nobody budgets for, and it's why we check the instrument before we trust the number.

submissions.title: Anti-Conjugate
submissions.description:
AntiConjugate is a safety layer for AI-assisted ADC prescribing research.

Antibody-drug conjugates combine complex biology, narrow safety margins, organ-function constraints, and high-risk drug interactions. Standard language models can produce fluent answers while inventing trial citations, accepting false premises, or missing critical contraindication signals in elderly patients with polypharmacy.

AntiConjugate addresses this with a dual-stage architecture:

A Generator drafts an evidence-backed risk card from ADCdb, openFDA, and NHS chemotherapy protocols.
A separate Neutral Estimator checks whether the draft may have missed a must-flag risk.
Uncertain or high-risk cases are blocked and routed to human clinical review.
Every claim must resolve to a real source; unsupported citations are rejected.
The system explicitly rewards “I don’t know” rather than confident guessing.
On a 30-item clinician-verified benchmark, AntiConjugate achieved:

+18.0 vs. −93.0 TruthRL score
0.040 vs. 0.425 Brier calibration score
100% abstention on trap cases
0 fake citations
Safe escalation of uncertain edge cases to human clinicians
AntiConjugate is not a replacement for a prescriber or pharmacist. It is an auditable safety layer designed to make AI-generated clinical reasoning more cautious, falsifiable, and accountable before it reaches a human decision-maker.

submissions.title: Attempt at Bettering the NetMHCstabpan
submissions.description:
Peptide–HLA complex stability predicts T-cell immunogenicity better than binding affinity, yet the standard predictor — NetMHCstabpan (2016) — is a sequence model whose accuracy degrades with distance from its training alleles. We asked whether structure-based foundation models (Chai-1 co-folding + full-atom LigandMPNN) could improve on it, split two ways: (a) augment — can a structural signal patch NetMHCstabpan's blind spot on isolated alleles? and (b) replace — can a purpose-built structural pipeline predict stability on its own?
Our answer is no — and we provide the evidence for it. To make the strongest possible case for structure, we hand-engineered features explicitly aimed at escape kinetics — weakest buried anchor, two-ended clamp, burial, and rigidity — then stress-tested them under strict leave-one-allele-out evaluation on a pre-registered 15-allele panel, plus a zero-shot external probe on a never-seen allele type (HLA-C; the external target is melting temperature, a thermodynamic endpoint). (a) On isolated alleles structure is competitive — it matches-to-modestly-beats the fair LOAO baseline by rank — but the gain is not concentrated where the sequence model is blind (our pre-registered distance gate fails), and against the deployed model it is within noise. (b) The standalone pipeline recovers only an affinity-scented signal a sequence model already captures.
Crucially, the ceiling is upstream of the feature engineering: the best signal came not from our purpose-built kinetic features but from Chai-1's generic interface-confidence scalar (ipTM), and the entire feature space collapses to ~2 correlated axes — so no further feature on the same static pose can add independent signal. The mechanism we infer explains why: these models report well depth — an equilibrium (affinity) quantity — whereas the stability endpoint we care about, dissociation half-life, is governed by the escape barrier, a kinetic quantity they never emit, because they only ever produce a single static bound pose. We cannot fully separate affinity from kinetics in our data, and argue (from the models' training target, not a multi-model experiment) that the limit is categorical to this model class — structure prediction + inverse folding.

*PS: We used Modal for the entirety of the challenge - apologies for not noting above. we are in A HUGE RUSH RN

submissions.title: PMDB - Which Batch Made This Electrode?
submissions.description: PMDB identifies which manufacturing batch a battery electrode came from, using SEM cross-sections of silicon-graphite anodes. The obvious approach fails in an instructive way: an intensity model scores 71% in cross-validation, then changes its answer when you add one grey level of brightness, because it learned the microscope settings rather than the material. We measured what actually differs between batches (where the silicon sits through the coating depth, not how much of it there is), ran 68 finite-element charging simulations to confirm composition alone can't explain it, and then found the dataset's hidden structure by stitching the 34 "independent" images back into the 13 parent electrodes they were cropped from. That discovery dictated the final model: a linear probe on MicroNet patch embeddings, validated leave-one-parent-out so sibling crops can never leak between training and test (0.71 accuracy, permutation p = 0.005). Everything runs live in a browser dashboard that matches the Python pipeline to 1e-15.

submissions.title: RecodeX
submissions.description:
RecodeX: infrastructure for autonomous sequence optimisation

RecodeX is a closed-loop infrastructure for autonomous biological sequence optimisation. It provides the machinery needed to iteratively generate, evaluate, validate, and improve DNA sequences under user-defined biological constraints.

At its core, RecodeX turns sequence design into a search problem over an enormous combinatorial sequence space. Starting from a wild-type sequence, the system generates candidate variants, evaluates them against an optimisation objective, rejects candidates that violate biological constraints, and feeds successful solutions back into the search process.

submissions.title: PARALLAX
submissions.description:
**Parallax is an opportunity-mapping and observability layer for scientific AI and automated labs.**

Most scientific AI reasons inside the dataset it is given. **Parallax reasons about how to expand what science can observe.**

It maps the opportunity space around an experiment in two directions: first, by finding new scientific handles that may already be latent in existing data — markers, representations, relationships, spatial or morphological descriptors — and second, by identifying what the current experiment cannot observe at all, from chemistry and 3-D structure to larger spatial scales or alternative imaging modalities.

Parallax then connects those blind spots to the measurement capabilities that could make them observable, creating an evolving map of **what we know, what else we can extract, what remains invisible, and what may be worth measuring next.**

For this hackathon, we demonstrate the concept on microscopy data. Statistical challenge, provenance reconstruction and agentic literature search turn a single dataset into a map of candidate markers, evidential limits and new measurement opportunities.

The goal is not simply to optimize the next capture. It is to help scientific agents discover **new observational handles and new regions of the research landscape**.

**Find what to measure next.**

submissions.title: Mendel Evolve
submissions.description:
MendelEvolve: Genetics for Algorithm Discovery. Evolve ideas, not programs, and measure what each idea is worth.

AI systems such as AlphaEvolve rewrite whole programs and keep the high scorers. They find good algorithms, but afterwards nobody can say which idea produced the result. MendelEvolve turns every idea a language model proposes into a gene: a named switch in the solver, with a stated hypothesis. LLM agents only invent ideas; classical search tunes and recombines them with no LLM calls; and knockouts (switching one idea off on fresh, paired seeds) give each idea a measured effect with an interval. The resulting ledger explains every result.

Results from the weekend:
- New lower bounds at 17 sizes of problem 60 from Tao and co-authors (no five points on a sphere), each verified by three independent exact checkers, and posted on DeepMind's record thread.
- 58-point sets with no isosceles triangle in the 32 × 32 grid, where two papers state 56 is optimal; DeepMind's own verifier accepts them.
- The best known circle packing (n = 26) from OpenEvolve's own starting program, with no hints. One gene carries it: knocking it out costs 1.67.
 - The knockouts on our own records, measured at scale (600 paired runs per idea), showed that the best single idea was one the engine's quick screen had rejected.

Ten problem packs (five added by outside agents from the docs alone), a protocol for adding more, and a live dashboard with knockouts are in the repo.

submissions.title: Graderade
submissions.description:
Graderade

AI models learn by iterating on tasks that a grader marks automatically. If the grader has a hole, the model learns the hole. Today, people catch these by reading tasks one at a time, or a single AI call reads the task once and gives an opinion.

Graderade is an AI agent that reviews training tasks before they ship. It works inside the task's environment with the full task, the grader and the models' attempts. It tries to break the grader the way a cheating model would, then tries to disprove its own flags before keeping them.

In a medical interview task, it found that the grader never reads the treatment plan, so a note that withholds the life-saving drug still scores 9 out of 9. In a botany task, it found that the grader never checks what the model actually looked at on each plant.

On 67 real tasks humans had already reviewed, 72% of its flags were right. Every critical flag comes with a measured score as proof.

Built by [name], [name] and [name] at Originator, for post-training teams.

submissions.title: Fail Better: Teaching AI Scientists to Falsify Their Discoveries
submissions.description:
We build tools that help AI science agents distinguish biological discovery from misleading predictive success.

Our test case is longevity: can DNA explain why some species live much longer than others? Using aMASS for dataset discovery and Devin and Claude for implementation, we built a DNA-to-lifespan model using 1,871 vertebrate species, reaching r ≈ 0.67 on held-out species. It looked promising—but what had the model actually learned?
We challenged it with a shuffle-input falsification test: scramble DNA-token order while preserving token composition. Correlation remained substantial at r ≈ 0.46, revealing that much of the predictive signal survived disruption of sequence order. A strong score was not enough to demonstrate that the model had learned mechanisms controlling lifespan.

We turned this experience into two reusable deliverables: a shuffle-based evaluation benchmark and an MCP-accessible Book of Genomics Failures. The book combines documented failure cases with executable checks for data leakage, sequence similarity, confounding and simple-baseline performance, helping agents challenge their results and design better experiments.
Guided by this failure-aware approach, we redesigned the analysis around DNA → predicted gene activity → longevity associations, using Genomic Intelligence models. Across a 48-mammal dataset, our initial screen identified 30 candidate gene associations; follow-up sequence shuffling weakened the associations in all six candidates tested. We also built an exploratory lifespan-prediction tool, while explicitly distinguishing comparative associations from causal mechanisms and reliable human predictions.

submissions.title: PepShield
submissions.description: PepShield asks whether a peptide–HLA stability predictor can tell you when to distrust it. We train on the Rasmussen 2016 SPA dataset (28,166 measured half-lives, 5,633 unique 9-mers, 75 HLA alleles, all A and B) and predict `log10(half-life + 0.1)` with a small MLP, comparing three feature sets: BLOSUM50 peptide plus a one-hot allele, frozen ESM-2 embeddings, and a "pocket" encoding that replaces the one-hot with the BLOSUM50 profile of the 34 NetMHCpan groove-contact residues. On top of that we run a five-member bootstrap ensemble and fit a split-conformal quantile on held-out calibration alleles, so every prediction ships with a 90% interval and a statement about whether the allele and peptide were in training. The result we actually care about is the failure mode: on peptide-disjoint data the system works and the interval covers 89% of the time, but on a genuinely unseen allele the ranking collapses to Spearman 0.17 and the ensemble's own disagreement stops tracking the error, which the pocket encoding improves (median 0.19 vs 0.06 across eight held-out alleles) and a heteroscedastic variance head does not. We present this honestly rather than hiding it: NetMHCstabpan scores 0.86 on the same file but was trained on it, so we label it in-sample rather than calling it a beaten baseline, and the live demo at <https://sarah04menla--demo.modal.run> deliberately withholds a numeric interval for HLA-C*07:02 instead of inventing one. The interface puts the prediction first, then shows the five ensemble members, the calibrated interval, and an AlphaFold view of the binding groove, keeping those three quantities conceptually separate because only one of them is a calibrated statement about error.

submissions.title: Project BirdNest
submissions.description:
Project BirdNest is a formally verifiable autoresearch framework for discovering algorithms for open construction and optimisation problems.

Recent systems demonstrate complementary strengths: AlphaEvolve uses LLM-guided evolutionary search and improved best-known constructions on several of 67 mathematical problems; ProofCouncil uses author–critic collaboration and produced correct or near-correct solutions on 6/10 FirstProof problems; and Aletheia uses long-horizon generate-verify-revise loops, including autonomous solutions to four open questions.  

BirdNest combines these ideas while targeting weaknesses we identified in existing autoresearch workflows:
Specification drift: An agent can silently misinterpret a difficult problem into an easier one and then successfully optimise for the wrong objective. BirdNest introduces Lean formalisation as a specification layer before research begins. This follows the broader move toward formally grounded research represented by Formal Conjectures, which now contains 1,029 open research conjectures formalised in Lean 4.  
Non-deterministic scoring function generation: Bespoke Source-to-Source Lean compiler for deterministically generating a fixed-interface Lean program used as the candidate scoring function for the main autoresearch loop. 
Cost and latency: We fine-tuned Qwen specifically for natural-language to Lean formalisation, moving a recurring specialist task away from expensive frontier-model inference, reducing cost and increasing performance.
Poor research traceability: Every hypothesis retains its parents, mechanism, implementation, experimental result, failures, objective score and cost. The output is therefore not merely the best program, but an inspectable research lineage showing how it was discovered.
LLM self-evaluation: LLMs generate ideas and critique results, but fixed deterministic evaluators decide validity and performance. 
Connecting previous work: Multi-agent BirdNest allows you to maintain a ledger of all problems that you have worked on, so that interesting approaches from different problems can be easily connected and shared!
The resulting pipeline is:
Problem → Lean Formalisation → Lean Compiler → Diverse Idea Generation → Implementation → Deterministic Experiment → Elite Archive → Evidence-Grounded Critique → Evolution

Our novelty is therefore not another single-agent wrapper around an LLM. BirdNest integrates formal specification, deterministic Lean compile checks, diversified evolutionary search, deterministic evaluation and complete experimental provenance into one autonomous research loop. BirdNest evolved through the same evidence-driven process it applies to research: profiling led us to fine-tune Qwen to reduce formalisation costs, while observed search convergence motivated diversified elite preservation. We also expanded from a single problem type to multiple problem families, enabling agents and researchers to reuse insights across problems and collaborate through a shared, growing research record. We deploy our system and run inferences using Modal to keep it compact.

submissions.title: LabForge
submissions.description:
LabForge: an epistemic digital twin for autonomous labs. Describe the lab you want in plain English. A Claude agent asks what it doesn't know, picks real instruments from scraped vendor catalogues, lays out the room with safety zones and human operators, and prices a full bill of materials. A discrete-event Monte Carlo simulation then turns every throughput claim into a range and names the bottleneck. LabForge also optimises running labs with what-if sweeps, orders a project queue, and writes the orchestrator skill file an AI agent would need to run the lab.

What makes it different is that it tries to prove itself wrong. An independent verifier re-runs every design and falsified our own chemistry agent's claims. Its cost band caught 14 of 18 published autonomous labs. On LabDesignBench, our reward-hacking benchmark, it passed 81% of checks against 66% for Claude without tools, with better calibration (Brier 0.048 vs 0.192). Every pipeline draws on 20 published protocols.

Sponsor tech: Anthropic Claude (Opus) is the planner agent and tool-use loop, and Claude Code built and integrated the codebase across five people. Amass provides literature evidence that every design step cites. Modal is wired in as an optional compute backend.

Links: GitHub https://github.com/WTreyde/virtual_labs
Demo https://huggingface.co/spaces/wtreyde/labforge

submissions.title: Antigen Presentation Stability: Sequence Is All You Need?
submissions.description:
We investigated whether pretrained protein models improve prediction of peptide–HLA dissociation half-life—a measure of how long a peptide remains bound for immune recognition.

Using 28,166 measured peptide–HLA pairs across 75 alleles, we compared a supervised sequence ensemble with frozen ESM-2 embeddings and Boltz-2 structure-derived features. The sequence ensemble achieved median per-allele Spearman correlation of **0.706** on the test split. ESM-2 showed no demonstrated worthwhile gain, while the tested structural pipeline performed worse (**0.595**). ProteinMPNN inverse folding and FoldX energy calculations were explored as diagnostic pilots.

The sequence model also transferred to an independent immunopeptidomics dataset, distinguishing naturally presented peptides from proteome decoys with median **AUROC 0.966**. Our contribution is a reproducible comparison of predictive accuracy and compute cost, including informative negative results.

Technologies used: **Modal** for cloud compute on **NVIDIA GPUs**, **OpenAI Codex** for scientific review, Python/PyTorch, ESM-2, Boltz-2, ESMFold2, ProteinMPNN and FoldX.
